accepted.question_text: Let S be a semigroup and let X be any set. A semigroup conjugacy relation on S is partition-covering if, for every partition of X, one can put a semigroup structure on X whose conjugacy classes are exactly the blocks of that partition. For the standard semigroup conjugacy relations ∼o, defined by a ∼o b when there exist g,h in S with ag = gb and bh = ha; ∼p, defined by a ∼p b when there exist u,v in S with a = uv and b = vu; and ∼tr, the epigroup relation defined using idempotent powers a^ω and b^ω together with elements g,h satisfying ghg = g, hgh = h, hg = a^ω, gh = b^ω, and ga^(ω+1)h = b^(ω+1), must every partition arise as the set of conjugacy classes of some semigroup?

evidence.quote: To investigate whether some analogous structure exists for semigroups, Problem 6.10 from [3] asks whether the conjugacies studied therein are partition-covering.
Theorem 3.3. ∼o, ∼c, ∼n, ∼p, ∼p∗, and ∼tr are partition-covering.

accepted.question_text: For semigroup elements a and b, define a ∼p b to mean that there exist u and v in the semigroup with a = uv and b = vu. If a semigroup embeds into a group, must this relation ∼p be transitive on that semigroup?

evidence.quote: Since free semigroups are embeddable in groups, Problem 6.4 asks whether ∼p is transitive for any semigroup that can be embedded in a group.
Corollary 5.2. There exists a semigroup that is embeddable in a group for which ∼p is not transitive.

accepted.question_text: For semigroup elements a and b, define a ∼p b when there exist u and v in the semigroup with a = uv and b = vu. If a semigroup has the property that ∼p is transitive in every variant of that semigroup, where the variant at an element c has multiplication x ◦ y = xcy, must ∼p already be transitive in the original semigroup?

evidence.quote: Problem 6.22 from [3] asks whether ∼p must be transitive for a semigroup if it is transitive for all of the semigroup’s variants.

This example is generated by {5, 6, 7} with the following properties: (1) 5 · 6 = 5 · 7, (2) 6 · 5 6∼p 7 · 5, and (3) any word of length at least 3 equals 0. (1) and (2) imply ∼p is not transitive for S, but (3) implies ∼p is transitive for every variant.

accepted.question_text: Is there any semigroup conjugacy relation that is not partition-covering, meaning that there exists some partition of some set that cannot be realized as the conjugacy classes of a semigroup for that relation?

evidence.quote: A natural question to ask at this stage is whether there are any semigroup conjugacies that are not partition-covering. Indeed there are.
Since the identity element will always be in its own conjugacy class, ∼u cannot be partition-covering for any set with more than one element.
